source.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
source.authors: Ian Magnusson; Noah A. Smith; Pang Wei Koh

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps language-model size and training-token budgets, measures held-out cross-entropy, and fits loss-scaling functions. It applies this scaling measurement to OLMo-core models and to COUNT, a different training architecture.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted scaling relationships for LM validation loss and downstream task loss, and compares compute-optimal fitted losses. Other results about RAM use, throughput, table swapping, and n-gram implementation are not results on the claim versions and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study assumes the Hoffmann-style form L = E + A/N^α + B/D^β, fits it to each arm, and uses the fitted compute-optimal curves only to express COUNT's gain as equivalent extra compute (46–89% LM loss, 6–56% task loss). It reports no fitted exponents or coefficients, no goodness of fit, no check that loss follows a power law, and no extrapolation or allocation results. The scaling law is a measurement tool for the study's own method, which is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that COUNT, using precomputed host-RAM n-gram counts with no added learned parameters, matches standard transformers trained with 46–89% more compute on LM loss and 6–56% on task loss. The abstract cites 57% at 1B. They also conclude it beats learned n-gram embeddings under GPU-memory limits and enables training-free domain adaptation via table swapping. They make no claims about the scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameter/token scaling sweeps and held-out loss measurements, but applies them to an OLMo-core ladder and a COUNT n-gram input-embedding method rather than reproducing either original study’s exact model and training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model size and D/N budget; COUNT also varies with table capacity and n-gram settings. The study reports sensitivity to inference-time candidate count K and retained orders J, embedding amplification, and the embedding basis, but those ablations do not establish the claim’s fitted scaling exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding frozen host-memory n-gram count embeddings shifts the fitted compute-optimal loss curve. The baseline would need 46–89% more compute to match LM loss and 6–56% more to match task loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-parametric memory augmentation shifts the compute–loss scaling frontier by a roughly constant compute multiplier.

record.problems: Fitted coefficients and exponents are not stated in the supplied text; key per-run loss and accuracy values are presented in figures rather than as numerical tables. The tested model range is 60M–1B, and no held-out extrapolation test is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-size and D/N plotted points were not extracted separately; the reported fitted scaling relationships are recorded as ladder-level results. Other COUNT ablations and results on RAM, throughput, table swapping, and domain adaptation are outside the listed claim versions. Relevant scaling plots and details are in Sections 4–5 and Figures 1–5, 9, and 12–18.

untested.parts: Power-law form is assumed for fitting, not tested; no exponents or fit quality are reported.
Compute-optimal curves are used, but optimal N and D versus compute are not reported.
Not tested; the ladder co-varies depth and width with size.
Task loss is fit with the assumed form; predictability is not evaluated.
Not tested. The parameter-counting convention (N excludes input embeddings, includes head) is stated but not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling fits serve only to quantify the method's gain. The study is reclassified from T1/tests to T4/uses_without_test, and all rows are unlinked. COUNT's table capacity grows with backbone size (17.1 GB for 60M–190M, 797 GB for 370M–1B), so the COUNT arm's curve mixes parameter and memory scaling. The 60M–1B range and the 1e18–1e20 FLOP compute range are both narrow.

versions.untested_parts: The reported sweep covers 60M–1B backbone configurations and D/N values of 10, 20, and 40; it does not establish the law across a much wider range of model sizes or tokens.
No reported test checks whether fits to small runs predict separately held-out, orders-of-magnitude-larger runs.
The study selects compute-optimal fitted losses but does not report how the optimal parameter and token counts individually scale with compute or compare their growth exponents.
No controlled comparison varies depth or width at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law test is reported for other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study fits downstream task loss and reports accuracy across its tested model ladder, but does not establish predictability for other downstream metrics or settings.
The study does not test how fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations change under alternative parameter-counting conventions, fitting procedures, schedules, or data.
